Patrick 1/20/2026 6:35 PM
For thirteen moons, your people had held off the invading goblin horde. The city of Berriksburg, capital of the Berrik province, had long ruled the rolling farmlands, richly wooded forests, and ferried many workers to the mountains for mining. One day Duke Larg Berrik received word that a small army of goblins had taken over a farmstead in the far northern reaches of the province. He immediately dispatched forty soldiers to exterminate the threat and recover the land, only to discover the small army was just the invading tip of a much larger, more bloodthirsty horde. Only ten people came back from that mission to report on the massive invasion force that was steadily marching southward, burning villages and abducting citizens as goblin slaves. They marched first from the north, held back by the Rivenglow river temporarily until they constructed a sturdy bridge of bones; those of your fellow citizens and soldiers; to cross it. The northern villages were evacuated to the safety of the Keep's walls before the rampaging armies could get to them, thankfully. Carrier pigeons were sent to neighboring cities and communities, asking for aid in repelling the invasion lest they be next; unfortunately only two pigeons returned with good news: the dwarven colony of Helmcrest in the southern mountains your city frequently traded with, and the elven village of Langerglim deep in the eastern forest that had already experienced goblin scouting parties in their territory and didn't wish to be next on the chopping block. Many refugees started arriving at the city gates with graphic, harrowing tales of the debauchery and sheer brutality of the goblin forces. The dwarven citadel of Helmcrest dispatched a unit of 100 soldiers to help defend the city, and Langerglim sent a squad of 50 scouts and snipers to aid the Duke in defending the city.
6:35 PM
Within six months another force comprised of a mixture of orcs and goblins began capturing territories in the west, including most of the arable farmland; and within the last month they've started attacking from the southern mountainous region as well, a dire sign that the Helmcrest dwarven clan the city had been allied with for so long had succumbed to the monstrous invasion. The skies grew darker with greasy smoke day by day, and more and more refugees clambored for the safety of the strong stone walls of the Keep, thinning the already widely spread resources even more. On one particularly bitter winter night, the scouts reported bonfires in every direction. The Keep of Berriksburg had been surrounded, and the enemy was steadily approaching. The clergy prayed for protection, casting wards upon the walls in the names of their gods, and the hedge wizards and runecasters crafted hexes and potions to prepare for the inevitable. Any able person was trained in sword, spear, and bow to defend the last bastion of civilization left in the province. It took two weeks before the thunder of war could be heard, like a low rumbling on the horizon from every direction; a mixture of guttural war cries, the uneven rolling of siege weaponry wheels, the crunch of bones as the weak were trampled by the mighty.
6:36 PM
Fortune looked lost, and hope was thin, but Duke Berrik would not let his people languish in apathy. He called on his closest advisors, Marmillian the court wizard, Silvik the Army General, and Amelya his spiritual advisor, and gathered them along with the remaining noble houses in the city to begin crafting plans to hold out for an extended siege. Emergency farms were started in whatever spare dirt was available. Water was carefully rationed, and cisterns built to store captured rainwater for when the river would become inevitably tainted. Every forge in the city was set to creating weapons and armor with a dwarven smith directing every hammer, and every hedgewizard with even a drop of magical talent was commissioned to create scrolls and enchant as much equipment as possible. Scouting and saboteur parties were disappearing much more often, and finally the Duke had decided it was not worth the loss of life to continue sending them out. Soldiers started to sing goblin slaying songs as they practiced, lead by their elven cohorts, as a means of keeping their spirits high when death came to visit their stone castle walls.
6:36 PM
And it visited with a fury so far completely unknown to anyone in the city, in the form of flaming boulders raining down upon the walls, and the chopping of hundreds of axes upon the iron portcullis. The walls were manned day and night with archers and spell flingers, slaying as efficiently as they could until exhaustion; their relief being a lukewarm meal and a mug of ale, and a light story of their childhood to distract from the death consuming all around them; before a tireless sleep and waking up to repeat the process. To rally hope for a victory, Duke Berrik himself would up a spot upon the walls, killing as many goblins as he could. But one day a flaming boulder collapsed the part of the wall he was stationed on, and he fell into the rabid hunger of the goblin hordes, and was pulled into pieces and devoured to the horror of onlookers. That outer wall was also breached that day, and General Silvik quickly rallied troops to fight off the invaders and help evacuate as many as possible into the interior Keep walls. Mounted forces were sent out, but very few returned. The troops on the outer walls were ultimately abandoned and assumed lost as new defenses were rallied to the inner walls to protect what little was left to protect. Hope was lost almost entirely as even the clerics tired prayers fumbled carelessly out of their mouths. The heavy wooden gate that was the final barricade was being assaulted by hundreds of axes, splinters flying everywhere, and the fevered cries of what could only be thousands of goblins reached a hellish pitch as the night descended upon the doomed city of Berriksburg.
6:36 PM
Until the red glow bathed everyone in blinding light. Through the darkness of night, a brilliant red light had beamed down upon the entire city. The invading forces were undeterred, and continued their frenzy, when in the blink of an eye it all stopped. Birds chirped overhead, the goblins that had managed to get through the gaps in the nearly shattered gate looked around confused as they were without their reinforcements, and thus their will to fight vanished. The red light had dissipated, and looking up one could see a dim red sun shining mercilessly down. There was little time to ponder; the remaining goblins were captured and sent to the dungeons, the Duke's foppish son Drake had reluctantly claimed his father's title, and the survivors finally took a pause to rest. Time was difficult to gauge however, as the sun never moved from it's fixed position directly overhead, never rising or setting or even dimming. It has been half a day since the Keep has been mysteriously transported to what can only be called a valley. Outside of the walls a lush forest can be seen, with plateaus in the northwest, vast marshlands to the southeast, and a river winding around the Keep fed from an impossibly tall waterfall to the far north. A reddish haze permeates the distance, allowing visibility of about three miles. Marmillian and Amelya have gathered several of the most capable survivors together to form expeditions to explore this new land. You are one of them.
6:40 PM
You are standing in front of the young, newly anointed Duke Drake Berrik, who has not even had the time to grieve his own father's death just a day before. His carefully trimmed, bearded face betrays his lack of readiness for the fate thrust upon him, but it is easy to determine he is trying his absolute best.

Axiom does not wait for discussion. The moment the last beastman hits the ground, the steel paladin is already moving. One clean step forward. A few, economical arcs of the greatsword. Armor pounds through brush and fern, branches snapping and whipping aside as Axiom vanishes into the forest with relentless purpose, the severed head swinging low at their side. The sound of their passage fades quickly, swallowed by trees and distance. Only the aftermath remains. The message is clear—even without the head still attached: This was not rage. This was intent.

110 feet away. Through smoke. Through chaos. Through the clash of steel and the sight of Oryn falling. Axiom Ferrum does not run. They advance. Each step deliberate. Heavy. Measured. The sound of armored weight compressing earth carries through the clearing like a drumbeat of inevitability. The greatsword comes free from their back with a long metallic rasp that cuts through the battle noise. They do not shout immediately. They let the beastmen see them first. A towering silhouette of scarred steel walking straight toward a twin-bladed brute that just dropped one of their own. Then— Their voice rolls out, amplified by helm and fury alike. “You have drawn blood.” Another step. “You stand in stolen land.” Another. “And you face consequences.” The blade lowers to their side, point dragging briefly across stone, sending sparks into the dark. “You mistake numbers for strength.” “You mistake size for dominance.” Their optics flare brighter. “I have shattered giants.” “You are not giants.” The words are not screamed. They are delivered like verdicts. Axiom turns their helm slightly toward the party without breaking stride. “Hold the line.” “Breathe.” “They bleed.” “They fear.” “You are not prey.” Back to the beastmen. “Drop your weapons.” “Kneel.” “Or I will demonstrate why your sentries did not return.” The final words ring like a hammer strike. “Choose quickly.” And Axiom keeps walking.

The distance closes. Ninety feet. Sixty. Thirty. The large beastman turns, twin greatswords rising, nostrils flaring at the advancing wall of steel. Axiom does not slow. The greatsword comes up in both hands. Their voice lowers into something resonant—measured, liturgical. “Prime Artifice.” Runes along the blade ignite—dim at first, then blazing—light coursing through engraved channels like molten circuitry. “Witness this recalibration.” The air tightens. The weapon hums with contained force. “You raised steel against my allies.” Ten feet. “Now feel sanctified steel.” The beastman roars and swings— Axiom steps inside the arc and brings the blade down in a brutal two-handed cleave. Radiance detonates— —and meets nothing. The brute twists with shocking speed, crossing its twin blades as it pivots aside. Axiom’s smite crashes into the earth instead, blasting soil and roots apart in a blinding surge of weaponized light. The ground splits. The beastman remains standing. For half a heartbeat the clearing is daylight. Then darkness surges back. Axiom holds the follow-through, blade buried in shattered soil, holy energy crackling and fading along the steel. Slowly, they wrench it free. Their voice is steady. Clinical. “Adjustment required.” They reset their stance, optics locking onto the brute’s center mass. “Speed exceeds projection.” “Strength confirmed.” “Durability… pending.” The sword rolls once in their grip, embers still licking along the fuller. A step forward. Deliberate. “You evaded correction.” A faint tilt of the helm. “That was the warning strike.” Their shoulders square. “The next one is instructional.”

The others disappear into the dark, their shapes swallowed by stone and echo. Axiom Ferrum remains. They do not pace. They do not fidget. They lower themselves slowly onto a flat stone just inside the veil of mist, greatsword laid across their knees—not resting, merely waiting. The waterfall’s roar crashes endlessly beside them. To most, it would be deafening. To Axiom, it is data. Rhythm. Pattern. Interruption detection. Their helm tilts slightly as they recalibrate auditory filters, isolating anomalies from the constant thunder. A falling rock. A bird taking flight. The shift of distant weight across gravel. The construct exhales once—a soft venting of internal heat. A gauntleted thumb runs along the edge of their blade, not sharpening, not polishing—just confirming integrity. The radiant channels engraved in the steel are inspected with mechanical patience. “Edge stable.” They look outward into the forest beyond the falls. The trees sway. Mist coils. For a moment, their posture softens—minutely. “Perimeter intact.” Axiom reaches up and adjusts a dent in their chestplate left by earlier combat. The metal does not yield easily. They press until it aligns closer to intended geometry. “Structural deviation within acceptable tolerance.” Silence again. Then, quieter—almost to themselves: “You are not permitted to fall yet.” The words echo faintly in the helm—memory, not current speech. They shift slightly, ensuring the cave entrance remains fully within their field of view. Listening. Counting breaths between thunder. Waiting for a whistle that does not come. And if something approaches— It will find not a resting guardian— —but a wall that happens to breathe.

Their voice carries low through the thunder of water. “This territory is temporarily occupied.” A measured pause. “We seek no claim.”** The blade lowers until its tip rests flat against stone—clear, non-threatening posture without surrender. Yoshi Exotic
Axiom Ferrum
Thirty minutes. No breach. No whistle. No hostile return. Only waterfall. Mist. And the persistent, exploratory nudging of a juvenile owlbear attempting to conquer a sword three times its size. Axiom Ferrum does not react when the cub paws at the flat of the blade. They simply adjust the weapon’s angle—two degrees—so the edge never faces the animal. “Bladed surfaces are not recreational objects.” The cub gnaws experimentally at the crossguard. Axiom rotates their wrist, denying leverage without force. “Teeth integrity: inferior to tempered steel.” Eventually, the cub settles. Its weight presses against Axiom’s armored foot as it sleeps. The construct does not withdraw. “Load increase: negligible.” When the mother returns—fish clamped in her beak—Axiom’s optics track the movement but their posture remains unchanged. No challenge issued. No threat posture assumed. The cub wakes and feeds. The sound of tearing flesh mingles with the roar of water. Axiom watches the treeline beyond them, not the meal. “Perimeter remains secure.” A faint pause. “Coexistence protocol successful.” Mist rolls past steel and feather alike. After a moment, Axiom speaks quietly—less declaration, more observation. “Predators who feed their young do not seek unnecessary conflict.” Their gaze shifts briefly toward the cave’s darkness behind them. “Let us hope the same holds true for what waits inside.” And so Axiom waits— Sword steady. Cub at their foot. Mother eating. An unlikely guardian at the threshold of two worlds.
